comparator.name: Communication and Information Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: The documented 2026–2027 Media and Journalism allocation totals 180 EC, including 30 EC of approved open study. This is a qualified comparison of that published academic content, not a certified progression route for 2026 entrants. Discourse and Social Interaction requires Discourse Analysis, which is absent from the route allocation. The applicable prerequisite, any extra credit or replacement, and consequent thesis access remain unverified. Future 2027–2028 and 2028–2029 recruitment revisions are provisional and are not substituted into this comparison. Adopted 2026–2027 OER Article 9.1 and the exact annual course list require a pass in Discourse Analysis before Discourse and Social Interaction. The first course is in the English Language and Media route but is absent from the Dutch Media and Journalism allocation. The published Formuleren course overlaps in discourse methods, but its explicit use as an entry requirement is for Interactie in Organisaties. Article 3.7 allows an individual examination-board exemption, not a cohort rule. The provisional 2027–2028 recruitment list omits Discourse and Social Interaction and lists Digital Deception and Redactionele innovaties, without an adopted replacement, credits or cohort bridge. The shown allocation has 60 EC each year, including 30 EC open study and a 12 EC thesis and colloquium pair. OER 9.1 requires passing all first- and second-year courses for the thesis and colloquium. The Dutch diagnostic and any required remediation gate Academic Skills, and 42 EC plus the designated skills and language conditions apply to ordinary first-year study advice. Orientation and language requirements add no credits. Open study has approval and level rules. Workshops and practicals normally require 80% attendance.

routeSelection.basis: The registry target is Dutch-taught, and the adopted 2026–27 OER names Media en Journalistiek as the only current Dutch-taught specialization. The two English routes and closed teach-out routes do not match this target; the selection follows formal target identity, not UCR fit.

core: Media change, representation and audiovisual narrative
Empirical research, data and critical source assessment
Journalism, public life, institutions and ethical judgment
adjacent: Public trust, misinformation and democratic institutions
Data, AI and technical understanding of digital media
questions: How do media forms, language and institutions shape public knowledge?
How can research and responsible communication evaluate contested information?

alternatives.label: Media, narrative & public storytelling
alternatives.labelReason: Study how moving images, language and stories shape public understanding. Combine media history, rhetoric, close textual and visual interpretation with qualitative and quantitative inquiry, documentary interviewing and production. VU provides a dedicated newsroom, journalistic writing, conversation-analysis and thesis sequence beyond this broader media-studies response.
alternatives.concept: Study how moving images, language and stories shape public understanding. Combine media history, rhetoric, close textual and visual interpretation with qualitative and quantitative inquiry, documentary interviewing and production. VU provides a dedicated newsroom, journalistic writing, conversation-analysis and thesis sequence beyond this broader media-studies response.
progression: Foundational media, language and social inquiry lead into advanced persuasion, documentary and independent interpretive projects. Research Methods precedes Experimental Statistics. Actual planned offerings and all formal prerequisites were checked against the current workbook.

alternatives.label: Media, misinformation & public trust
alternatives.labelReason: Investigate how media and institutions shape public trust. Study persuasion, social influence, democratic and European institutions, ethical argument and misinformation. Use empirical research, fact-checking and documentary practice to assess public claims. This is a related direction, with climate and American media cases that do not reproduce a journalism degree.

alternatives.distinctness: The organizing focus is Media, misinformation & public trust. It changes 37.5 EC each way from the closest programme; the changes form a coherent subject/method strand, rather than a threshold-based substitution.

alternatives.label: Data, AI & digital media inquiry
alternatives.labelReason: Connect critical media study with the analysis of data and digital systems. Develop R-based inquiry, database and SQL knowledge, image-processing practice and statistical learning alongside rhetoric, documentary work and AI ethics. These provide technical understanding relevant to changing media; a dedicated data-journalism newsroom, news recommender or media-engineering project is not guaranteed.
alternatives.concept: Connect critical media study with the analysis of data and digital systems. Develop R-based inquiry, database and SQL knowledge, image-processing practice and statistical learning alongside rhetoric, documentary work and AI ethics. These provide technical understanding relevant to changing media; a dedicated data-journalism newsroom, news recommender or media-engineering project is not guaranteed.
progression: Foundational media, language and social inquiry lead into advanced persuasion, documentary and independent interpretive projects. Research Methods precedes Experimental Statistics. R-based data foundations precede Machine Learning; image-processing and SQL supply a distinct technical strand.
alternatives.distinctness: The organizing focus is Data, AI & digital media inquiry. It changes 30 EC each way from the closest programme; the changes form a coherent subject/method strand, rather than a threshold-based substitution.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Required first-year development with scholarly source evaluation and written argument.
Designs empirical studies, creates instruments and analyzes results in R to support audience and media research.

Applies fairness, privacy and accountability frameworks to AI and uses research-grounded podcast communication. It adds analysis of AI in public communication without claiming recommender engineering.
Actual relational theory, SQL, normalization, authorization and query processing support a distinct data-infrastructure strand; no journalism project is inferred from the description-only evidence.
Imports, cleans, analyzes and visualizes data in R. Those methods support evidence-based storytelling, while no newsroom dataset or editorial workflow is assumed.
Actual supervised and unsupervised statistical learning, resampling and held-out evaluation in R/Python support understanding digital data systems; no dedicated news recommender is promised.

Actual Python/OpenCV filtering, segmentation, feature detection and recognition-pipeline evaluation explain computational image analysis. This is technical media inquiry, not audiovisual journalism or recommender training.
Fact-checks, investigates statistical misrepresentation and misinformation circulation, and produces a researched debunking video.
Analyzes ethical arguments and applies moral frameworks to practical questions. This supports reasoning about media responsibility without implying journalism-specific law.
Develops normative analysis of rights and political authority using original texts. This frames questions about democratic public debate.
Investigates democratic institutions and participation through empirical comparative methods. This supports analysis of media in democratic settings.
Uses agenda-setting, representation and legislative evidence to study institutional politics, supplying a concrete policy setting for public communication.
Studies networks, identity and stratification to interpret differences in audiences and public participation.
Uses interviews, focus groups and documentary methods for qualitative audience and communication inquiry.
Investigates civil society, trust and public spheres through an independent research project.
Studies persuasion, social influence and group processes and develops a theory-based research proposal.
Develops experimental-design knowledge and multivariable analysis, with transferable methods for communication-effects research.
Teaches persuasive argument and storytelling through rhetorical analysis, written exercises and public speech.
Analyzes language, discourse and stylistic choices in literary and nonfiction texts, with original textual analysis.
Uses climate communication as a sustained case to analyze contested public messages and the forms that carry them.
Practices speaking, debate and storytelling through a community teaching project, contributing communication practice.
Tests framing, argument and audience-sensitive persuasion in community-engaged work.
Develops close reading and analysis of narrative, style and form, with introductory film adaptation.
Analyzes life narratives, ethical representation and digital self-presentation, with written practice and independent analysis.
Studies how narratives change between text and film through formal analysis, adaptation theory and a substantial project.
Applies contrasting interpretive perspectives to text-based research.
Develops close analysis of moving images, film narrative and audiences with analytical or creative-analytical practice.
Investigates the material and historical forms of media, including an independent object study.
Uses American television, film and digital media to investigate representation, identity and narratives.
Applies close media analysis to the representation of science, risk and ecological questions, with an analytical or media project.
Analyzes media power and representation through American examples, archival research and documentary podcast practice.
Practices nonfiction audiovisual production and assesses documentary representation, interview and editorial choices.
blocks: VU explicitly introduces journalism as a research field and public practice. UCR moving-image foundations are relevant but do not constitute that dedicated journalism introduction.
UCR media archaeology examines technologies and historical communication; no equivalent current media-use research course is asserted.
Dedicated journalism theory-to-practice preparation is distinct from the UCR media and documentary courses.
VU requires newsworthy journalistic articles, verification, sources, editorial teamwork and peer revision. UCR life writing and documentary work do not supply this complete newsroom writing sequence.

Both combine critical audiovisual interpretation with research, interviewing, filming and editing. VU explicitly produces journalistic reels, reportage and explainers; UCR produces a short documentary and studies nonfiction form and ethics.

Both analyze narrative techniques across media. UCR examines medium specificity and literary-film adaptation through a substantial project; VU studies news narratives, truth claims, ethnographic content analysis and membership categorization, which remain distinct.
Both examine how language and textual choices construct meaning. UCR emphasizes stylistics, grammar, cognition and discourse; the complete VU introductory media/communication remit differs.
UCR stylistic and qualitative inquiry contribute relevant analysis. The dedicated standardized written/spoken discourse-analysis and formulation sequence is not duplicated.
Both connect communication and public life. UCR studies public spheres, civil society and empirical public initiatives; VU gives journalism and democracy a dedicated focus.
Both examine persuasion, audience, framing and ethical message choices. UCR applies these through actual community communication and reflective research; contexts and assessments differ.
No full communication-and-cognition counterpart is asserted. UCR stylistics and psychology make narrower contributions elsewhere.

VU teaches inductive conversation analysis, turns and social actions using natural/institutional talk. UCR qualitative/discourse and interviewing work does not establish this specialist sequence; formal entry also remains unresolved.
UCR Ethics makes a real philosophical contribution, but a complete counterpart to the external philosophy course is not established by the retained evidence.
VU applies institutional conversation analysis to journalistic, legal and healthcare interaction. UCR interviews/discourse inquiry are relevant but do not reproduce that dedicated analytical method.
UCR empirical methods and persuasion are relevant; no complete dedicated communication-effects research sequence is asserted.
Ethics, AI responsibility and documentary representation provide contributions, but no dedicated journalism/media-ethics course is asserted.

VU studies cognitive processing of visual/verbal messages, advertising metaphors and instructional images. UCR close visual and persuasive analysis is relevant without duplicating this cognitive-method sequence.
Both develop empirical social-research design and quantitative inquiry. UCR includes surveys/experiments, R analysis and an actual group research project; institutional methods sequences differ.
Both develop academic inquiry, writing, presentation and reflection. UCR adds civic and personal development; it does not implement the VU language-test and remediation gate.
UCR uses writing across research courses, but no scheduled course is asserted as the dedicated VU academic-writing course.

Both find, transform, analyze and visualize numerical/textual data. UCR uses R and multiple data types, including web data; VU additionally requires a newsworthy journalistic story and high-quality visualizations. That editorial formation is not supplied by data methods alone.

Both support empirical statistical inference. UCR applies multivariate regression, ANOVA, logistic and factor methods in R with research reporting; communication-specific applications and the preceding methods sequence differ.
Genuine approved 30-EC open study remains uninstantiated; level/approval restrictions and any consequence of the missing prerequisite are not replaced by invented choices.

VU conducts practice-relevant empirical research for media/journalism organizations. UCR has actual empirical/community projects, but no guaranteed commissioned media-organization research course is supplied.
Required thesis symposium organization, presentation and public-science output are distinct; UCR presentations do not certify this culmination or its access conditions.

VU requires an individual thesis with a work plan, GO/STOP decision and independent second reading. Optional UCR research is additional to the scheduled 180 EC and cannot close this required thesis difference.

selection.assessment: Three independently supported directions: closest media/narrative inquiry; public trust and institutional communication; data/AI understanding of digital media. Their 37.5,30,37.5 EC pairwise differences arise from coherent methods and subjects. Stop at three; no additional career-only or platform-example programme is generated.

notes.text: VU provides dedicated journalistic writing and audiovisual news production, conversation analysis, communication-effects inquiry, commissioned media research and a required thesis/colloquium. UCR offers broader media, rhetorical and empirical study with real documentary work. Its climate and American media cases are specific contexts; its technical alternative does not guarantee data-journalism, news-recommender or newsroom training.
VU’s selected Media and Journalism route is Dutch-taught, with some shared teaching in English. The UCR programs are taught in English; they do not certify Dutch journalistic writing proficiency.

acceptance.claim: Actual UCR media, language/rhetorical, documentary and empirical inquiry supports a broader comparison with VU’s documented 2026–2027 Media and Journalism content, with distinct public-trust and data/digital-media related directions. This does not reproduce the complete journalism, conversation-analysis or thesis formation or certify a complete cohort pathway.
acceptance.targetContext: VU Communication and Information Studies, Dutch Media and Journalism route; documented academic year 2026–2027.
acceptance.challengeMethod: Separately identified same-AI source-first final pass against adopted OER, actual annual course content and current UCR evidence; no separate model or human endorsement.

uncertainties.fact: The adopted OER and current annual Discourse and Social Interaction page require passing Discourse Analysis, absent from the Dutch route table. The thesis and colloquium require all first- and second-year courses. Future recruitment revisions are provisional, with no adopted replacement/credit bridge.

adverseResolutions.resolution: Discourse Analysis is an additional compulsory course whose credits displace open study or another allocation, or a different preparatory course is formally imposed.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: The allocation and unrestricted elective capacity are not certified. More specialized discourse preparation may increase the already explicit specialist gap. The published media, language, journalism and empirical subjects and the actual broader UCR response remain independently supported; no exact conversation-analysis or full-degree equivalence is claimed.

adverseResolutions.resolution: An authoritative cohort-wide equivalence, waiver or corrected prerequisite permits the published sequence.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: No waiver is assumed. It would resolve access without changing the confirmed current subject/method content or the broader, explicitly limited UCR response.

adverseResolutions.resolution: An adopted revised cohort removes the disputed course and introduces distinct innovation, deception or social-media methods, changing advanced weighting and thesis preparation.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: Those future changes and a complete 2026-entry progression are excluded from this current 2026–2027 content comparison. No claim is made that the current allocation predicts that future route. The demonstrated response to the currently documented media/narrative, journalism, public-information and research content remains valid within the stated boundary.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Communication and Information Studies examines language, media and communication. Its Media and Journalism route combines media analysis, rhetoric, journalism practice, research methods and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: This qualified comparison addresses VU’s documented 2026–2027 media, language, journalism and research content. UCR offers broader media and documentary study, plus related public-trust and data/AI directions. VU’s dedicated journalism, conversation-analysis and thesis formation remains distinct. An unresolved prerequisite affects formal progression; this comparison does not certify a complete cohort pathway.

componentNotes.y3-01: Approved open 30 EC, subject to level/approval rules. Any displacement by an additional prerequisite remains unverified; unrestricted choice is not certified.
componentNotes.y2-03: The current entry requirement is a pass in Discourse Analysis. The route table does not list that prerequisite.
componentNotes.y3-05: A 3 EC parallel colloquium: organize a symposium, present thesis research and write a public-facing science piece. All components must pass.
componentNotes.y3-06: A 9 EC individual research thesis within a supervised theme group. Mandatory meetings, an approved work plan and a progress decision apply; supervisor and second reader assess independently.

comparisonScope.label: Qualified academic comparison
comparisonScope.assessed: The published 2026–2027 allocation: 180 EC, including 30 EC of approved open study. Academic content is assessed; formal cohort progression is not certified.
